title: Make a Presentation with a Message
subtitle: Craft a clear presentation that uses strong evidence.
objectives: Identify the main message and claims in a presentation.
Select credible evidence that directly supports each claim.
Organize presentation elements logically to build a compelling story.

scenes.title: What's Your Story?
scenes.display: Tell a story. Make it count.
scenes.narration: To persuade others, you need a clear message and solid proof. We learn to build powerful presentations, telling a story backed by strong evidence.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character gestures enthusiastically, then points to a thought bubble with a question mark and a lightbulb.

scenes.title: Message and Evidence
scenes.narration: Every presentation needs a main message. Evidence, like facts or examples, proves your points. This builds trust and makes your claims believable.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character holds a speech bubble, then adds smaller blocks labeled 'evidence' underneath it, making it look like a solid foundation.

scenes.title: A Reused Paper Initiative
scenes.narration: Propose a 'reused paper initiative' at school. Your evidence: 'We have 12 clean sheets ready.' This concrete proof supports your easy, helpful message.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character points to a simple slide showing 'Problem', then another showing 'Inventory (Evidence)', and finally 'Next Step'.

scenes.title: Key Elements
scenes.narration: An effective presentation has a clear message, specific claims, and strong evidence. A logical structure guides your audience from problem to solution.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character reviews a checklist appearing on screen: 'Main Message', 'Claims', 'Evidence', 'Structure'.

scenes.title: From Weak to Strong
scenes.narration: A weak presentation might just say, 'Reusing paper is good.' Improve it by adding evidence: 'It saves trees, and we collected 12 sheets already.'
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character first shows a flimsy, empty box, then replaces it with a sturdy box filled with visible 'evidence' blocks.

scenes.title: Plan Your Presentation
scenes.display: Outline Your Idea. Find Your Proof.
scenes.narration: Now, plan your presentation. Choose an idea, identify your main message, and list your claims. Brainstorm specific, relevant evidence for each point.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character holds a blank whiteboard, then a pencil and paper appear, ready for planning.

scenes.title: Share Your Story
scenes.narration: You've learned to craft presentations with clear messages and solid evidence. This skill helps you communicate effectively, showing your ideas are well-founded.
scenes.visualAction: A cartoon character stands confidently next to a projector screen displaying a completed presentation outline.

reading.title: The Power of Evidence
reading.text: A presentation with a message needs a main idea and claims. Evidence is the proof that makes your claims believable. It can be facts, examples, or observations. Without evidence, your message is just an opinion. With it, you build trust and show your ideas are well-founded.

reading.title: Example: Reused Paper Initiative
reading.text: To propose a 'reused paper initiative,' you might claim it's easy and helpful. Evidence could be '12 clean sheets of paper already collected' or 'three volunteers ready to help.' This specific proof makes your proposal strong and shows it's achievable.

reading.title: Evaluating Your Evidence
reading.text: Good evidence is relevant, specific, and credible. Ask: Does this proof directly support my claim? Is it clear and easy to understand? Can I show where this information came from? Strong evidence makes your message powerful and convincing.

promptExamples.initial: Tell me about your presentation idea.
promptExamples.improved: What is the main message of your presentation, and what specific evidence will you use to support each of your claims?
promptExamples.followup: How does the evidence you chose directly connect to and strengthen your claim about [specific point from their presentation]?

activity.title: My Presentation Plan
activity.instructions: Create a short presentation plan for an idea you have. First, state your main message. Then, list at least two claims that support your message. For each claim, describe the specific evidence you would use. Finally, explain why you chose to order your presentation parts this way.
activity.starter:
My Presentation Idea: 
Main Message: 
Claim 1: 
Evidence for Claim 1: 
Claim 2: 
Evidence for Claim 2: 
Order Explanation:
activity.expectedEvidence: A written plan including a main message, at least two claims with specific supporting evidence for each, and a brief explanation of the presentation's logical flow.

quiz.question: Which of these is the BEST example of evidence for the claim: 'Our school needs more recycling bins'?
options: Recycling is good for the environment.
I saw three overflowing trash cans with recyclable items in the cafeteria today.
Many students agree that we need more bins.
quiz.explanation: Option B is the best evidence because it's a specific, observable fact that directly supports the claim. Option A is a general statement, and Option C is an opinion, not concrete proof. (Source: concept)

quiz.question: You are presenting an idea for a 'Healthy Snack Day' at school. Which piece of information would be the MOST effective evidence to support the claim: 'Students will enjoy these healthy snacks'?
options: A survey showing 80% of students prefer fruit over candy.
A picture of a delicious-looking apple.
A general statement that healthy food tastes good.
quiz.explanation: Option A provides specific, measurable data from a relevant source (a survey of students) that directly supports the claim about student enjoyment. Option B is visual but not evidence of preference, and Option C is a subjective opinion. (Source: example)

quiz.question: A student claims: 'Our class project will be the best.' Which question would help them improve their presentation by adding stronger evidence?
options: What makes our project unique and how can we prove it?
Who else thinks our project is good?
quiz.explanation: Option B prompts the student to identify specific qualities of their project and consider how to provide proof for those qualities, which is key to strengthening the evidence. Option A is too general, and Option C relies on opinion rather than concrete evidence. (Source: check)

mission.title: Propose a New Club
mission.instructions: Imagine your school wants to start a new after-school club. Choose a club idea (e.g., a coding club, a book club, a nature club). Create a short presentation proposal (2-3 slides) for this club. For each slide, clearly state its main point and provide specific, imagined evidence to support it. Remember to organize your points logically.
rubric: The presentation has a clear, central message about the club.
Each claim made about the club is supported by specific, relevant, and imagined evidence.
The presentation flows logically from one point to the next.
The evidence provided is distinct from mere opinions or general statements.

hints.question: What kind of evidence can I use?
hints.answer: Evidence can be facts you've observed, examples you've found, or even simple data. For instance, if you're proposing a 'nature club,' evidence could be '5 students expressed interest in a nature walk last week' or 'our school has a garden that needs care.'

hints.question: How do I make sure my evidence is strong?
hints.answer: Make sure your evidence is specific and directly related to your claim. Instead of saying 'everyone likes it,' say 'a survey of 20 students showed 15 prefer this idea.' Specific numbers or observations are stronger than general statements. (Source: check)

hints.question: How should I structure my presentation?
hints.answer: Start with the problem or opportunity, then introduce your idea (your main message). Follow with claims supported by evidence, and finish with a clear next step or call to action. This creates a logical story. (Source: concept)

educatorNotes.sampleAnswer:
For the 'My Presentation Plan' activity:
Main Message: Our school needs a 'Green Team' to improve recycling.
Claim 1: There's a lot of recyclable waste going into regular trash.
Evidence for Claim 1: I observed 5 classrooms and found 3 had overflowing trash bins with plastic bottles and paper mixed in.
Claim 2: Students are interested in helping the environment.
Evidence for Claim 2: In an informal poll, 10 out of 12 classmates said they would join a 'Green Team' if it were easy.
Order Explanation: I started with the problem (waste) to show why a Green Team is needed. Then I showed student interest to prove it's a feasible idea, ending with a call to action.

For the 'Propose a New Club' mission:
Title: Coding Explorers Club
Slide 1: Problem/Opportunity
Main Point: Many students want to learn coding but don't know where to start.
Evidence: Last semester's 'Tech Week' coding workshop had a waiting list of 20 students.
Slide 2: Our Solution: Coding Explorers Club
Main Point: A club offers a fun, easy way to learn coding basics.
Evidence: We have access to 5 laptops in the library and free online coding tutorials that are beginner-friendly.
Slide 3: Next Steps
Main Point: Let's start small and grow.
Evidence: We can meet once a week for 45 minutes, and I've already found 2 teachers willing to supervise.
educatorNotes.commonMisconception: Students often confuse opinions or general statements with concrete evidence. They might say 'everyone likes this idea' instead of providing specific data or observable facts.
reviewChecks: Does the presentation have a clear main message?
Are there at least two distinct claims supporting the message?
Is specific, relevant evidence provided for each claim?
Is the evidence distinct from personal opinions or general statements?
Does the explanation for the order make sense?
educatorNotes.safetyNotes: Remind students that when gathering 'evidence' in real-world scenarios (like polls or observations), they should always do so respectfully and without disrupting others or collecting private information. If they are observing others, they should do so discreetly and only in public spaces.
